title: Water cycle
examples: What are the main steps in the water cycle?
Does the water cycle happen on the moon?
Can you show me a diagram of the water cycle?

explain.say: Today we learn about the water cycle. It shows how water moves around Earth. First we look at evaporation. Evaporation is when liquid water turns into a gas called water vapour. Say this with me: evaporation.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: the water cycle. Look at the sun, the evaporation and the condensation. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
Next is condensation. Condensation is when water vapour cools down and changes back to tiny liquid water droplets. Think about the cool morning air. This is condensation happening.
The third step is precipitation. Precipitation is when the water droplets in the clouds get too heavy. They fall back to Earth as rain or snow. This is precipitation.

items: Rain, snow, or hail reaches ground

explain.say: In our everyday lives, the water cycle is always working. Think about a puddle drying up on a sunny day. The sun causes evaporation from the puddle. This is the cycle in action.
A common mistake is thinking the water cycle only happens in the ocean. Remember that water can cycle in rivers and lakes too. All bodies of water participate.
The whole process repeats over and over again. This continuous movement is what we call the water cycle. It keeps all life on Earth going.

faq.q: Why is it called a cycle?
faq.a: It is called a cycle because the steps repeat in the same order. Water moves from one stage back to the next constantly. You might also hear it called the water loop.

faq.q: What is the difference between evaporation and transpiration?
faq.a: Evaporation is water turning to gas from surfaces like puddles. Transpiration is when plants release water vapour into the air. They are both ways water enters the air.
asks: Is plant water part of the cycle?
What is the gas from plants called?

faq.q: Does the water that falls as rain come from the same water?
faq.a: Yes, the water is constantly recycled. The water that falls today might have rained here hundreds of years ago. This is why we call it the water cycle.

faq.q: What causes the water vapour to cool down enough to form clouds?
faq.a: As the warm, moist air rises higher, it meets cooler temperatures. This cooling causes the water vapour to change back into liquid droplets. This is the process of condensation.

faq.q: Is the water cycle only about liquid water?
faq.a: No, it includes all three states: liquid, gas, and solid. We see liquid in rivers, gas as vapour, and solid as ice or snow.

facts: Evaporation is the process where liquid water turns into water vapour.
Condensation is the process where water vapour cools and forms liquid droplets.
Precipitation includes rain, snow, sleet, and hail falling from clouds.
The water cycle has no true beginning or end.

quiz.say: When water vapour cools and forms clouds, what process is happening?
quiz.why: Condensation is the correct term for gas turning back into liquid droplets.

wrong.1: Evaporation is when liquid turns into gas, which is the opposite process.
wrong.2: Precipitation is when the water falls from the cloud, not when it forms.
wrong.3: Collection is where the water gathers, but it is not the name of the cooling process.

quiz.say: Sunlight heats up a large puddle, causing water to rise as vapour. Which step is this?
quiz.why: The sun's heat turning liquid water into vapour is the definition of evaporation.

wrong.0: Precipitation is the falling of water from the sky.
wrong.1: Cycle is the name of the whole process, not the specific action.
wrong.3: Condensation happens when the vapour cools and turns back into liquid.

quiz.say: If clouds become too heavy and release rain, what is this action called?
quiz.why: Precipitation is the scientific term for water falling back to Earth from the atmosphere.

wrong.0: This is not the standard scientific term used for the falling water.
wrong.2: Evaporation is water going up into the air, not falling down.
wrong.3: Condensation is the process of forming the cloud, not the falling of the water.
